title: Leading Change Without Splitting the Church
subtitle: The change that split the last guy's congregation, the pace that does not, and the patience it will cost you to move people instead of running them over

sections.title: The Change That Split the Last Guy
sections.body:
Ask the older members why the church is wary of you, and somewhere in the answer is a man who came before you and broke something. He had a good idea. He may have been entirely right. He changed the music, or the service times, or the way the elders were chosen, and he changed it fast and he changed it over the top of people who were not ready, and the church split, and families who had worshiped together for thirty years stopped speaking, and he left, and the wound is still in the room when you stand up to preach.

He was probably right about the change. That is what makes the story tragic instead of simple. Being right is not the same as leading well, and a man can be correct about the destination and catastrophic about the road, and the people he ran over will not remember that he was right. They will remember that the church died of his rightness.

This is the inheritance you walk into. Every congregation has a scar like this, and the scar is not irrational. It is memory. Before you change one thing, find out what the last change cost them, because you are not introducing change to a blank room. You are introducing it to people who have already bled once and have promised themselves they will not bleed again.

sections.title: You Spend Trust to Buy Change
sections.body:
Every change you make is a withdrawal from an account, and the account is trust, and most new leaders do not know how little is in it when they arrive. They preach for six months, they feel beloved, they mistake the honeymoon for a fortune, and then they make a withdrawal the size of a mortgage and the account bounces and they cannot understand what went wrong.

Trust accrues slowly. It is built by the funeral you preached for a man you barely knew but honored anyway, by the hospital visit at midnight, by the year you stayed when you could have left, by the small promises kept until people stop bracing for you to break one. Change spends it. A small change spends a little. A change that touches what people hold sacred, the music, the building, the way it has always been done, spends a great deal, and if the account is empty the change does not happen. The church only revolts and you only learn, too late, the true balance.

So the order matters, and most leaders get it backward. They lead with the big change because it is the reason they came, and they spend trust they never accumulated. The wise leader makes deposits for a long time before any large withdrawal, and makes the early changes small and obviously good, the ones that build the account rather than draining it. You are not just changing things. You are managing a balance, and the balance is the difference between a church that follows you and a church that splits.

sections.title: Move at the Speed of the Slowest Sheep You Love
sections.body:
There is a speed at which a congregation can change without tearing, and it is almost always slower than the leader wants and faster than the leader fears. The art is finding it, and the only way to find it is to actually know your people, not your strategy, your people, the particular ones in the particular pews with the particular histories.

The widow in the third row whose husband built the cross that hangs behind you is not an obstacle to your vision. She is a sheep, and her resistance to change is not stubbornness. It is grief, and love, and a fear that the church she is about to die in will become a place she no longer recognizes. You can run her over. It will be efficient. It will also be a sin, because she is one of the ones Christ died for, and the leader who sacrifices the weak for the sake of the vision has confused the kingdom with a corporation.

Move at a pace that does not leave her behind. This will infuriate the young and the eager, who are right that the church must change and wrong that it must change now, this month, at whatever cost to the slow. Lead change like a shepherd moving a flock, not like a man driving cattle. The flock that arrives slowly arrives whole. The cattle that arrive fast arrive thinned, and the ones lost on the way were not obstacles. They were the point.

sections.title: Change the Why Before the What
sections.body:
Most failed change happens because the leader changed the practice before he changed the understanding. He moved the communion table before anyone understood why, and so the move looked like an attack on the old and not a service to the gospel, and people defend the old when they cannot see what the new is for.

Go slow on the why. Preach it, teach it, talk about it in living rooms and over coffee long before you ever propose the what. Let the congregation arrive at the conviction themselves, so that when the change comes it feels like the natural fruit of something they already believe and not like a decree from a man they are still learning to trust. People will accept almost any change they helped to reason their way into. They will resist almost any change handed down complete.

And bring the resisters in early, not late. The temptation is to avoid the people you know will object, to build your coalition of the willing and present the change as a done deal. This is how you make enemies. Go to the woman who built the cross first, before the decision, and ask her, honestly, what she fears. You may change her mind. She may change yours, and the change may be better for her objection. Either way she will have been honored, and a person who has been honored rarely becomes a person who splits a church. The split does not come from disagreement. It comes from people who concluded they did not matter.

sections.title: The Patience That Costs More Than Courage
sections.body:
We praise the courageous leader, the one who makes the hard call and takes the hill. We rarely praise the patient one, and patience is the harder virtue and the rarer one, because patience requires you to be right and to wait anyway, to see the destination clearly and to walk toward it at the speed your people can bear.

That is the cost no one warns you about. Not the courage to change. The patience to change slowly when you can see exactly where you want to go and exactly how long the slowness will take. You will watch the church limp toward something you could reach in a week if you were willing to break it, and you will choose the years over the week, and almost no one will know what that choice cost you, because the church you did not split is invisible. No one mourns the catastrophe that did not come.

Lead change like a man who plans to be buried in that churchyard. Slowly. Patiently. Spending trust you have actually earned, moving at the pace of the sheep you love, changing the why before the what, and honoring even the ones who fought you. Do it that way and you may not move as fast as you wanted.

But the church will still be standing when you are done. And whole. That is the whole point, and almost no one remembers it until the splitting is over.
